idiom_name: short method whose body is only calls to named private step methods
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: write the operations of the method as a sequence of calls to methods that do not exist yet, name each one after the step it performs, then implement the steps one level down. Keep the steps private to the unit that owns them (private member functions, package-scope functions, or module-scope helpers) and pass data through parameters and return values rather than shared state; if the steps need to share many locals, promote the computation to a Method Object instead. Recurse while a step is itself a composition, and stop when a step is no longer than its own signature or the sequence has stopped changing.
code_sketch:
run():
    reserve_stock()          # the body is the summary, one call per step
    charge_card()
    send_receipt()           # each step implemented one level down
pitfalls: Skipping the names again the first time a step needs a change - the composition only pays off while the calls stay calls.
Steps that accumulate parameters (or reach into shared state) until the coordinator's signature no longer describes the computation.
Decomposing a method nobody re-reads (generated code, throwaway scripts) buys indirection at no benefit.
Premature decomposition: extracting steps before the sequence is stable creates churn — decompose after the inline version has been read and understood, not before.
Macro methods that grow to more than 8–10 steps signal a misplaced abstraction boundary: the coordinator is describing multiple responsibilities and needs refactoring into collaborator objects.

Fragile ordering: when step methods have hidden order dependencies not expressed in their names, a reader cannot verify the sequence without tracing state — document ordering constraints in the coordinator's name or a comment.

Wrong move: extract every trivial statement into a method -> the coordinator becomes a list of wrappers with more indirection than meaning -> instead keep cohesive operations together and extract at semantic boundaries.

Wrong move: treat a pipeline or hook sequence as unconditional -> short-circuiting, rollback, and error paths disappear from the summary -> instead make control flow and cleanup explicit in the coordinator or use a construct that models branching.

Wrong move: expose every step as public for tests or overrides -> callers depend on implementation details and the step API ossifies -> instead keep steps private or protected and promote only deliberate extension points.
